explain.say: Smallpox once killed hundreds of millions of people. Today it is completely gone from the world. How? With an idea that started with milkmaids and cows. Let's travel along the timeline.

explain.say: Now 1796. Edward Jenner, an English doctor, noticed milkmaids who caught mild cowpox never got smallpox. He tested cowpox on a boy, who was then protected. The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow. Can you hear it?

faq.a: Variolation meant deliberately giving a healthy person material from a mild smallpox case, by a scratch or by blowing dried scabs into the nose. It usually gave a milder illness and lifelong protection, but some people died.
In 1796 Jenner took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and put it into a cut on James Phipps, aged eight. Later, Phipps did not catch smallpox. This was the first scientific vaccine.

The WHO led a global campaign from 1967, finding every case and vaccinating everyone around it, called ring vaccination. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, and smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.
asks: Tell me about smallpox being gone

faq.a: An mRNA vaccine carries instructions that tell your cells to make a harmless piece of a virus, such as its spike protein. Your immune system learns to recognise it. The mRNA breaks down within days.
Louis Pasteur in France. In 1885 he treated nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog, and the boy survived.

facts: Edward Jenner tested cowpox inoculation on James Phipps in 1796.
The World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.
Wild poliovirus cases have fallen by over 99% since 1988.
